feed.title: Receive screens and 'expiry': how users read payment-request expiry

entry.title: Receive screens and 'expiry': how users read payment-request expiry
entry.summary:
Many cryptocurrency wallets include an expiry attribute in payment requests, encapsulated within the URI alongside details like amount and label. This implementation has led to significant user confusion, as individuals often interpret the expiry as pertaining to the address itself, rather than the request. Such misunderstandings can result in users either panicking that funds sent to an "expired" address are permanently lost or erroneously abandoning an address that is still actively receiving payments.
The way information is presented appears to have a greater impact on user perception than the underlying technical mechanism. Tooltips, though intended to clarify, prove ineffective since many users simply copy the address without reading any supplementary guidance. This presents a challenge for wallet developers and maintainers when designing the receive flow, especially when considering whether it is necessary to display an expiry for standard on-chain payment requests at all, as opposed to only Lightning Network-style invoices where expiration is more relevant.
For wallets that do opt to show an expiry, finding clear wording that differentiates between the expiration of a payment request and the ongoing validity of the address is crucial to avoid misinterpretation. Furthermore, wallets that employ address rotation with each new request face the added complexity of communicating to users that previously generated addresses remain valid for receiving funds, despite no longer being featured in the active request interface.
These questions are driven by recurring support queries from users, highlighting the necessity for clarity and precision in both user interface design and communication around address and request expiry within wallet applications.
